summary: The Feyward Dan — the one-armed Shadowfell copy who had been sleeping through a collapsing library, a near-fatal duel, and an extradimensional crisis — woke up in a yellow bed on Estragon's Island, a magic school south of the Undead Swamps that ships supplies to the Mushroom Kingdom and the Regal Empire. He wandered the dormitories opening random doors and apologizing, encountered a female lightning orc professor of expression named Prismari who informed him that a surge of magical energy from Raventree Manor was amplifying emotional auras, learned he was on a small island with no money and no way to leave, was identified as a Toad in a place where Toads are not allowed, was slashed in the face by goblins, ran headfirst into a window, broke through on the second attempt, fell into a thornbush, was cornered by a Lorehold professor of chaos who tracked him with spotlights and a sniper, surrendered, was accused of opening the planar fracture, deflected blame onto God Toad and the Oracle, blinked and saw God Toad for one second, was presented with the captured Original Dan and told to choose which Dan lives and which dies, woke the Original Dan up, watched the Original Dan detonate a massive fire explosion that killed every goblin in the vicinity, was NOT protected by the Original Dan during the blast, swung a sword at the professor in desperation, took damage while the Original Dan took none, and then both Dans fled in opposite directions — Fey Dan wounded and running, Original Dan walking calmly away from a smoking crater without looking back, and the professor standing in the aftermath smiling and noting that this is an island and they will be caught eventually. Neither Dan has money. Neither Dan has allies. The exchange rate between gold pieces and Imperial Crown is favorable but irrelevant when you have zero of either.
description:
Waluigi has assembled this account from sources he is not entirely comfortable identifying, intercepted academic communications from Estragon's Island, and the kind of fragmented intelligence that arrives when someone falls through a dimensional boundary and lands in an institution that files attempted murder under administrative categories. The events described here represent the continuation of Dan's particular nightmare — not the Original Dan's nightmare, which is a separate and longer-running catastrophe involving cursed staffs, soul consumption, and Green T removing his arm, but the COPY Dan's nightmare, the Feyward Dan, the one-armed version who has been traveling with Disaster Inc. and sleeping through crises with the peaceful obliviousness of someone whose unconscious mind has correctly determined that consciousness is not currently worth the investment.

He woke up. Waluigi almost wishes he hadn't.

## Context: Which Dan Is Which and Why It Matters


Waluigi has documented the Dan situation across multiple articles and it remains, by his professional assessment, one of the most unnecessarily complicated identity crises in the entire Disaster Inc. orbit. But because this incident involves BOTH Dans meeting face to face for the second time and one of them detonating a crater, Waluigi will provide the essential context.

The Original Dan was once a decent leader of the Liberated Toads. He acquired a cursed staff. He killed thirteen of his own people. He nearly consumed their souls. Green T chopped off his arm. He was taken to an archmage for treatment involving dark magic. He became a second-class fire mage connected to the Mages' Guild, connected to Archie Miser, and connected to whatever organization produces Bowser Badges numbered up to at least 447. Bowser beat him nearly to death in the Corvinarus Sanctum approximately two to three days ago — or a month ago, depending on which plane's calendar you use, because time is broken and nobody has fixed it.

The Feyward Dan — also called the Shadowfell Dan, the fake Dan, the copy Dan, or 'whatever you call him' depending on who is speaking and how tired they are — is the one-armed version who has been traveling with the party. His origin is unclear. His relationship to the Original is unclear. Whether he is a copy, a duplicate, a temporal echo, a fey reflection, or something else entirely is unclear. What IS clear is that he has one arm, he was rescued from a Mazebound by Bowser in a tug-of-war, he slept through the duel in the Corvinarus Sanctum, and he just woke up on a magic school island with no money, no allies, and no idea how he got there.

The Original Dan, during the Grove of Woe incident, demanded: 'Hand over that Dan now. There can only be one.' This is a territorial claim over identity itself. Two Dans cannot coexist because identity is not a shared resource — it is a singular possession, and the Original views the copy's existence as theft.

Waluigi notes that the Original Dan killed thirteen Toads with a cursed staff and nearly ate their souls. The Feyward Dan has, to Waluigi's knowledge, not killed anyone. When the question of 'which Dan deserves to exist' is framed as a choice, the answer seems obvious to everyone except the people making the choice.

## The Yellow Bed: Waking Up Wrong


The Feyward Dan woke up in a yellow bed.

Waluigi will sit with this detail because it is the last moment of peace this Dan will experience for the remainder of the documented events. A yellow bed. Bright. Warm-toned. The kind of color that belongs to places where people sleep safely and wake up to breakfast and schedules and the mundane business of being alive. The yellow bed is a lie — not because it intends deception but because the environment it belongs to will attempt to kill the person sleeping in it within the hour.

Dan remembered what happened. The Mazebound. The grove. Bowser's roar. The tug-of-war that used his one remaining arm as the rope. The rescue.

'Bowser tried to save me,' he said.

Waluigi documents this because it matters. The Feyward Dan's first conscious thought after dimensional displacement was not confusion, not fear, not anger — it was RECOGNITION. Recognition that someone had fought for him. Bowser — the King of the Koopas, the man who commandeered Salam as a surfboard, the man who carries a letter to a dead princess and views every encounter through the lens of profit and punching — had grabbed Dan during the Mazebound engagement and pulled with the strength of someone who had decided this particular person was his to protect.

Dan's first thought was gratitude. His second thought, presumably, was 'where am I.' His third thought was probably 'why does my arm hurt.' His fourth thought should have been 'I need to leave immediately' but was not, because Dan is a Toad, and Toads investigate before they evacuate. This is why Toads keep getting into situations that require evacuation.

He got out of the yellow bed. He looked out the window. An island. Buildings arranged in the institutional pattern of dormitories or boarding houses. Studies laid about — instruments, books, the organized clutter of academic pursuit. People walking below, engaged in the business of a functioning institution.

Voices carried through the walls.

'I told you to get this project done by noon.'

'Don't worry, we can ship it to the Mushroom Kingdom in time.'

'Really? We are meant to ship it by today.'

'There are millions of battles at Rogueport. We will just tell them we got stuck in one. Besides, no Toads here for miles. No one will know.'

Waluigi needs to unpack the phrase 'no Toads here for miles.' It was said casually — the kind of workplace observation that functions as both logistical assessment and implicit warning. No Toads here. The absence is noted. The absence is EXPECTED. This is not a place where Toads are present, and the speakers' comfort with that absence suggests it is not accidental.

Dan — a Toad — was listening through the wall of a place where Toads are not supposed to be.

He did not process this warning. He read a journal instead.

## Silverquill and Gnash-Town: Academic Geography


The journal was titled 'Silverquill.' It detailed the location: Gnash-Town, on Estragon's Island. Waluigi has limited intelligence on Estragon's Island — it appears on certain nautical charts as a small landmass south of the Undead Swamps, associated with magical commerce and academic operations. The name 'Gnash-Town' suggests either a founding figure named Gnash, a history of dental problems, or an environment that makes people grind their teeth in frustration. Given what follows, Waluigi suspects the third option.

Dan left the bedroom and began opening random doors. This is the behavioral pattern of someone who is lost, has no plan, and believes that exploration will produce clarity rather than danger. In a dormitory at a school of magic on an island where Toads are not welcome, opening random doors is approximately as safe as opening random doors in Raventree Manor — which is to say, not safe at all, but Dan has been opening doors in Raventree Manor for weeks and has survived, so the behavior is self-reinforcing.

Each door produced an occupant. Each occupant produced a startled reaction. Dan said 'I'm sorry' to each one and moved on. He opened doors like someone checking hotel rooms for a friend who might be in any of them, apologizing his way down a corridor of strangers with the particular energy of a person who knows he does not belong but cannot figure out where he DOES belong.

Then he opened a door and found the lightning ogre.

## Prismari:


The Professor of Expression

Waluigi needs to correct the species identification in his sources. The entity behind the door is described as a 'lightning ogre' and subsequently as a 'female lightning orc.' Waluigi will use the term 'orc' because the subsequent conversation demonstrates intelligence, sophistication, and emotional perceptiveness that exceeds the typical ogre profile — though Waluigi acknowledges he may be engaging in species-based assumptions that his therapist would flag.

She was large. She was intimidating. Dan said: 'Sorry, didn't know it was occupied.' The response of someone who has already apologized to six strangers and has the phrasing on automatic.

She did not tell him to leave.

Dan decided to talk to her. Waluigi notes this decision as either brave or desperate — the calculation of someone who has opened every door and found no allies and has determined that the intimidating orc professor is, by process of elimination, his best available option.

'Sorry, looking around. Was curious,' Dan said.

'What are you curious of?'

'Don't know.'

Silence.

More silence.

The silence of two people who have nothing in common except proximity and the mutual recognition that the conversation has already failed by conventional standards.

Then she said: 'You're exuding a lot of colorful aura off yourself.'

She introduced herself as a professor of expression. Waluigi's intelligence on magical academic disciplines suggests this is a field concerned with the externalization of internal states — emotions, intentions, magical signatures rendered visible to those trained to perceive them. A professor of expression reads people the way Waluigi reads contracts: not for what they say but for what they REVEAL.

She asked what emotion he was expressing.

'Hmm. Annoyance,' she said, answering her own question. 'Maybe a tinge of patience.'

Annoyance and patience. Waluigi finds this reading deeply accurate. Dan has spent weeks traveling with Disaster Inc. — a group that shoots prisoners through doors, sings during stealth operations, and splits the party across dimensional boundaries because nobody can agree on priorities. Annoyance and patience are the BASELINE emotional state of anyone who has survived proximity to these people. Dan is annoyed at everything and patient with everything because the alternative to patience is screaming and the alternative to annoyance is despair.

Dan said he would get going. She said no — come in, shut the door.

'You're not from here, are you?'

Dan's response reveals the trust damage that Raventree inflicts on everyone it touches: 'Hmm, I just met you, but it depends — how do I know I can trust you?'

Her answer was devastating in its simplicity: 'Do you have anyone else to trust?'

'No...'

'Perfect.'

Waluigi needs to sit with this exchange. 'Do you have anyone else to trust?' is a question that only functions as persuasion when the answer is no. Prismari did not earn Dan's trust. She identified the ABSENCE of alternatives. Dan's trust was not given — it was defaulted to the only available recipient because the trust economy had collapsed entirely. He has no one. Not Bowser, who tried to save him but is stranded in a collapsing library. Not Markop, who is kidnapped somewhere in a cursed grove. Not Remi, who is heading toward the Tree of Woe without him. Not the Original Dan, who wants him dead.

Prismari is the only person talking to him. So Prismari gets his trust. This is not a decision. This is gravity.

She explained the magical disturbance. A surge of magical energy was causing her expressions — her professional tool, the thing she teaches — to become more expressive than intended. The amplification was annoying. The source was Raventree Manor.

'What's going on there?' Dan asked, lying.

Waluigi documents the lie because it is the CORRECT response. Dan knows what is going on at Raventree Manor. He has been inside it. He has been shot at, dragged by Mazebounds, rescued by Bowser, and displaced across dimensional boundaries because of what is going on at Raventree Manor. But telling a stranger on an unfamiliar island that you have firsthand knowledge of the magical catastrophe they are monitoring is the kind of honesty that gets you arrested. Dan chose deception. This is growth. Not MORAL growth — tactical growth. The kind that keeps you alive long enough for moral growth to happen later.

Prismari told him there had been a vote held by the Glazed Congress to investigate the situation at Raventree Manor.

Waluigi files the Glazed Congress under 'political entities requiring further investigation.' A congress implies governance. Governance implies jurisdiction. Jurisdiction implies that someone, somewhere, has the authority to DO something about the dimensional catastrophe unfolding at Raventree — and has responded to that catastrophe by holding a VOTE. A vote to investigate. Not an intervention. Not a response team. A vote. To determine what is happening. At a manor where the planar fracture has already been open long enough for a month of Shadowfell time to elapse.

Bureaucracy is the same everywhere. WAH.

## The Geography of Exile


Prismari showed Dan a globe. She pointed to a small island south of the Undead Swamps. That was where they were.

She got a doughnut globe — a different cartographic model, presumably accounting for whatever dimensional topology makes standard spherical globes inaccurate — and pointed to the Mushroom Kingdom. 'You're from here, right?'

'No, no. I'm Midlands.'

Dan had introduced himself: 'I'm Dan, from the Feywild.' And now he was clarifying Midlands. Waluigi notes the geography because it matters for what follows. The Midlands are not the Feywild. Wherever the Feyward Dan actually originates — whether his 'Feywild' designation reflects true origin or the dimensional transit that created or displaced him — he identifies his home as the Midlands. This is the first time, to Waluigi's knowledge, that the Feyward Dan has specified his geographic origin with this precision.

Prismari's reaction to 'from the Feywild' was a stutter. Then she muttered — quietly, possibly not intended for Dan to hear: 'You really are a danger to everyone around you.'

Waluigi needs to analyze this reaction. Prismari is a professor of expression — someone trained to read emotional and magical signatures. She has already noted Dan's 'colorful aura.' And upon hearing he is from the Feywild, she stuttered and called him a danger. This suggests that Feyward entities — or entities bearing Feyward signatures — carry recognizable markers that trained magical academics associate with danger. Not personal danger. Danger to those AROUND them.

Is the Feyward Dan a walking magical hazard? Is his aura — the colorful emissions Prismari identified — affecting the environment or the people near him? Is this why the planar fracture is being blamed on entities like him? Waluigi has insufficient data. But Prismari's reaction was involuntary — a stutter, a muttered assessment — and involuntary reactions from trained professors are more reliable than deliberate ones.

Prismari asked: 'You weren't a part of that, were you?'

'That' being Raventree. The fracture. The surge.

Dan's response was the negotiation of someone calculating how much truth is survivable: 'If I were, you wouldn't kill me, right?'

'Oh no,' Prismari said. 'The guards might have their way with you there.'

Not a denial of killing. A redirection of killing. SHE would not kill him. The guards — unnamed, unspecified, presumably the enforcement arm of whatever authority governs Estragon's Island — would handle that. Prismari was not offering safety. She was offering a buffer zone between Dan and institutional violence.

Dan tried to leave. The doors were locked.

Waluigi replays this sequence. Dan entered the room voluntarily. Prismari said 'come in, shut the door.' The door locked. Prismari then needed KEYS to open it — keys she retrieved with apparent helpfulness, smiling, saying 'oh dear me, I'll get that.'

Waluigi does not know whether the door locked automatically, whether Prismari locked it, or whether the building's security systems engaged upon detecting an unauthorized Toad. What Waluigi knows is that Dan entered a room, was told to shut the door, and then could not leave until the professor — the same professor who had just identified him as a danger to everyone around him — decided to unlock it.

'Oh, I got the keys. It's open,' she smiled.

Dan opened the door.

He was slashed across the face.

## The Goblin Hunt: No Toads Allowed


Goblins. The corridor was full of them. Dan ran. He tripped. He fell on his face — a sequence so consistent with the Toad experience of Disaster Inc. that Waluigi suspects it is physically encoded into their species at this point.

Goblins surrounded him.

'Wait, what's going on?'

'No Toads allowed.'

'Who reported me?'

The question answers itself, but Dan was not in a position to process the answer. Prismari had read his aura. Prismari had identified his Feywild origin. Prismari had called him a danger. Prismari had locked the door. Prismari had unlocked the door. Prismari had smiled.

The goblins were on the other side of the door.

Waluigi will not state definitively that Prismari orchestrated this. He WILL state that the sequence — identification, containment, release into a prepared ambush — is the operational pattern of someone who processes threats through institutional channels rather than personal action. 'Oh no, the guards might have their way with you.' She said this. Then the guards — or their goblin equivalent — were waiting at the door.

Prismari is a professor of expression. She reads people. She identified what Dan was and then she opened the door into what Dan would face. Whether this was deliberate betrayal or bureaucratic indifference — whether she SENT the goblins or merely KNEW they would be there — the practical result was identical: Dan was slashed and surrounded.

The goblin leader paused. Something Waluigi finds almost more disturbing than immediate violence: a pause. The goblins looked at Dan. Dan looked at the goblins. And then the goblin suggested — almost casually — 'Why not just let one Toad stay?'

This was not mercy. This was the negotiation of someone testing the parameters of policy. No Toads allowed. But what about one? What about an exception? The suggestion lingered for exactly long enough to create hope before another goblin answered: 'You're already causing a disturbance by being here.'

The leader snapped his fingers. Goons materialized behind Dan — the specific choreography of organized intimidation, the kind where the leader makes the pronouncement and the muscle confirms it.

'Rattle him, boys.'

Dan — Toad Lee, as the sources identify him — ran into a nearby room. He hit a window headfirst. The window did not break.

He hit it again. The window broke. Dan fell through the shattered glass into a thornbush below.

Waluigi needs to document this sequence with the precision it deserves because it encapsulates the Feyward Dan's entire approach to crisis management. He ran. He chose a window as his exit. The window refused to cooperate on the first attempt. A lesser individual — or a smarter one — would have reassessed after the first impact. Dan reassessed by hitting the same window a SECOND time with his HEAD. The window, presumably impressed by his commitment, broke. And then the thornbush, which had been minding its own business, received a one-armed Toad through its canopy at velocity.

Falling into a thornbush after breaking a window with your face on the second attempt is not an escape plan. It is a trajectory. Dan did not choose the thornbush. Gravity chose the thornbush. Dan merely provided the initial conditions — velocity, mass, desperation — and physics handled the rest.

## The Professor of Chaos: Lorehold Engagement


Guards surrounded the area below. A teacher emerged — big, black, bulky, carrying the particular authority of someone whose academic discipline involves breaking things.

A Lorehold professor of chaos.

Waluigi's intelligence on Lorehold College identifies it as an institution where archaeomancers draw magical power from the flow of time and fate. Professors of chaos specifically study breaking points — moments where the course of events can be fractured and redirected. They focus their magic into creating breaks to their advantage. Their attacks take the appearance of books, scrolls, and sheets of parchment — weaponized academia, which Waluigi finds both terrifying and oddly familiar.

The professor deployed magical spotlights — lights that tracked Dan's movement with the persistence of search beams, sweeping the grounds with the focused intent of someone who has done this before and finds it professionally satisfying. She called out to him with the warmth of a predator who has already won and is now enjoying the process.

'Oh, Toad. We won't kill you. Just please come out.'

She chased him. Dan climbed a tree. The professor stood below with the patience of someone whose entire discipline is based on waiting for breaking points.

'Come on, little Toad. The moment you run away is the moment I've got you.'

This is tactically accurate. Running from a chaos mage creates a sequence of events — a trajectory — and chaos mages specialize in identifying where trajectories break. Standing still offers no trajectory to manipulate. Running offers infinite breaking points. The professor was not threatening Dan. She was describing the nature of her power. She was telling him, in academic terms, that flight was surrender.

Dan tried to sneak up behind her. A sniper shot impacted next to him — the cracking sound of a projectile designed to miss by inches, the kind of warning shot that communicates 'we could have' without committing to 'we did.' The professor turned around. She was smiling.

'Any last words?'

Lights surrounded him. A sniper dot glowed on his body. The spotlights that had been sweeping were now focused — converged on a single Toad in a tree whose escape plan had consisted of hitting a window twice with his head.

Dan ducked. He dodged the light. He failed — the spotlight followed him with the mechanical inevitability of systems designed to track moving targets.

Dan surrendered.

'I'm sorry. I surrender. Do what you will.'

Handcuffs. The cold metallic reality of institutional capture — not the improvised restraints of Raventree, not the rope bindings of the tanuki incident, but proper handcuffs applied by an authority that has a SYSTEM for handling unauthorized Toads.

The professor's interrogation was efficient: 'Why were you at Raventree Manor?'

Dan explained. Waluigi's sources describe his explanation as 'somewhat unreliable,' which Waluigi interprets as meaning Dan told enough truth to seem cooperative and enough lies to seem innocent, producing an account that was neither convincing nor disprovable. This is the standard Toad interrogation performance — not good enough to deceive, not bad enough to provoke, existing in the gray space where captors decide whether further questioning is worth the effort.

A goblin emerged from the bushes. 'Gobber,' the professor called him. He had been tracking Dan with a device. The pursuit had not been improvised. It had been INSTRUMENTED. Dan's position had been known from the moment the tracking device was activated — possibly from the moment he arrived on the island. Every element of the chase — the goblins at the door, the spotlights, the sniper, the convergence — had been coordinated around a signal Dan was emitting without knowing it.

'Good work,' the professor told Gobber. 'The tracking device really worked.'

'Babhabhabhabhah,' Gobber said.

Waluigi does not speak goblin. But the tone was unmistakable: professional satisfaction.

## The Accusation: Planar Crimes


The professor's next statement repositioned the entire encounter from campus security incident to criminal investigation.

'You're wanted for magical crimes at Raventree. You come to me in particular — you're very brave.'

'You come to me IN PARTICULAR.' This phrase implies that the professor is not a random academic who happened to catch a trespassing Toad. She is SPECIFICALLY involved in the investigation of Raventree-related magical crimes. Dan did not come to her — Dan was delivered to her, through a sequence of events involving Prismari's identification, the goblins' ambush, and Gobber's tracking device. But the professor frames it as Dan's choice — 'you come to me' — because framing the suspect's capture as voluntary approach is an interrogation technique older than any college.

Dan asked what crimes specifically.

'Opening the planar fracture.'

The planar fracture. The dimensional rupture at Raventree Manor that has desynchronized time across planes, stranded party members in collapsing extradimensional libraries, enabled vampire wedding preparations, and produced the magical surge that Prismari identified as affecting her professional abilities. Someone — this institution, the Glazed Congress, whatever investigative body has jurisdiction — has determined that the planar fracture was OPENED. Not occurred. Not happened. OPENED. By someone. Deliberately.

And they think Dan did it.

'Oh, that. That's not me. That was someone else,' Dan said.

Then, with the particular audacity of someone who has nothing left to lose: 'Sorry, what's the planar fracture exactly?'

Waluigi marvels at this. Dan was just accused of opening the planar fracture. His defense is that he did not do it. His FOLLOW-UP is to ask what it is. This is either the most transparent lie ever told or the genuine confusion of a dimensional copy who may literally not know what happened at Raventree because he was ASLEEP through the critical events. The Feyward Dan slept through Bowser's duel with the Original Dan. He slept through the collapsing library. He slept through whatever portal sequence delivered him to Estragon's Island. It is entirely possible that Dan genuinely does not know what the planar fracture is because he was unconscious when it occurred and nobody briefed him when he woke up because nobody was THERE when he woke up.

'The ritual?' the professor prompted.

Dan maintained his denial even with the additional information. He did not do it. Someone else did.

'Then who did?'

'I don't know. I have a theory on who it might be, though.'

'Tell me.'

Dan named two suspects: God Toad and the Oracle.

Waluigi needs to address both names. God Toad is an entity Waluigi has encountered in fragmentary references — a figure of Toad theological significance whose nature, power, and relationship to mortal events Waluigi has not fully documented. The Oracle is the 46-year-old interdimensional custodian in the Corvinarus Sanctum, the flesh vat keeper, the figure Waluigi has never trusted and continues not to trust. Dan offered both names as potential suspects for opening the planar fracture.

Whether Dan actually believes either of them is responsible or whether he was deflecting blame toward entities too powerful or too obscure for the professor to verify is unclear. What IS clear is that naming God Toad and the Oracle as suspects in a magical crime investigation is the kind of statement that either ends an interrogation or escalates it dramatically.

It escalated it dramatically.

## God Toad: One Second of


Theology

The professor's reaction to the mention of God Toad was not surprise. It was not disbelief. It was PROCEDURE.

'You're about to meet God Toad,' she said.

'Neat,' Dan said.

Waluigi needs to hold the word 'neat.' Dan was just told he is about to meet a theological entity — a GOD, or at least an entity bearing the title of God — and his response was 'neat.' This is the response of someone who has been displaced across dimensions, hunted by goblins, shot at by snipers, accused of planar crimes, and has reached the emotional state where meeting God is filed under 'things that are happening' rather than 'things that should provoke existential crisis.' Dan has been through enough that divinity registers as mildly interesting.

'Just close your eyes,' the professor said. 'And he will come.'

Dan closed his eyes. He opened them — a blink, a fraction of a second, the smallest unit of visual perception available to mortal biology.

He saw God Toad.

For one second.

Waluigi cannot describe what Dan saw because Dan has not described what Dan saw and Waluigi's sources provide no detail beyond the fact of the sighting. One second. A blink. The briefest possible encounter with the divine — not a conversation, not a revelation, not a commandment or a prophecy or a burning bush. A glimpse. The visual equivalent of hearing someone say your name in a crowd and turning to find no one looking at you.

Did God Toad speak? Did God Toad acknowledge Dan? Did God Toad provide any information about the planar fracture, the Dan duplication crisis, or the tanuki's ongoing need for psychological intervention? Waluigi does not know. The encounter lasted one second. Whatever theology occurred in that second is Dan's alone.

Waluigi has opinions about gods who appear for one second. They are not flattering opinions. If you are a divine entity with the power to manifest before mortals, and you choose to manifest for ONE SECOND in front of a one-armed Toad who is handcuffed and accused of dimensional crimes he did not commit, you are either testing something, measuring something, or performing the theological equivalent of checking your mail — glancing at the contents, determining nothing requires immediate response, and closing the door.

God Toad appeared. God Toad was seen. God Toad left. Nothing changed. This is consistent with Waluigi's general experience of divine intervention: present enough to be documented, absent enough to be useless.

## The Choice: One Stays, One Dies


Rustling in the bushes. Movement. The organized noise of individuals approaching with purpose.

Goblins emerged holding the Original Dan.

Waluigi needs to establish the timeline. The Original Dan was last documented in critical condition in the Corvinarus Sanctum — beaten nearly to death by Bowser, his Bowser Badge ripped from his skin triggering immolation, cauterized by Bowser's own fire. That was approximately two to three days ago by Material Plane reckoning and possibly a month ago by Shadowfell reckoning. He is now here, on Estragon's Island, in goblin custody, conscious enough to be restrained and transported.

How did the Original Dan get from the collapsing Corvinarus Sanctum to Estragon's Island? Waluigi does not know. The portal that Bowser fell through was closed. The sigils were dead. But the Original Dan is here — recovered from near-death, mobile, and in custody. Either the sanctum had an exit that Bowser did not find, someone extracted the Original Dan before the collapse, or the Original Dan's connection to the Mages' Guild and Archie Miser's network provided resources for dimensional transit that the party does not have.

The professor presented both Dans with the clarity of someone who has done this before — the procedural confidence of an academic whose discipline involves breaking things and who has determined that the current situation requires something to break.

'Choose one. One stays. One dies.'

Waluigi has documented similar forced-choice scenarios in other contexts — the trolley problem as administered by people with actual trolleys and the willingness to use them. The framing is designed to externalize responsibility: the chooser bears the weight, the presenter merely facilitates. But in practice, the choice is theater. The presenter has already decided the outcome. The choice is offered to provide the APPEARANCE of agency where none exists.

Dan — the Feyward Dan, the copy, the one in handcuffs — asked to speak to the Original.

They allowed him.

Dan approached his other self. The Original Dan — the fire mage, the soul consumer, the staff-cursed leader who had killed thirteen of his own people — was restrained by goblins, battered from Bowser's beating, bearing the burn scars from the Bowser Badge's removal.

'Hello,' the Feyward Dan said. 'You may not know me, but you may know of me. But wake up.'

'Wah, what happened?'

'Hello, Original Dan. We're trapped and they're going to kill one of us off and let the other live.'

'What?'

'Ughh.'

'Damn that Bowser.'

'The Koopa soiled my power.'

Waluigi documents this exchange with the attention it deserves. The Feyward Dan addressed the Original Dan with formal distance — 'Original Dan,' acknowledging the primacy claim that the Original has always insisted upon. The Original Dan's response was not fear of death, not concern for his duplicate, not even confusion about the forced-choice scenario. It was ANGER AT BOWSER. The Original Dan's primary emotional response to being presented with his own potential execution was resentment toward the Koopa who had beaten him.

'The Koopa soiled my power.' This is the complaint of someone whose identity is inseparable from their capability. Bowser did not merely defeat the Original Dan — he DIMINISHED him. The beating was not just physical. It was categorical. A king with a warhammer and a portable cannon reduced a second-class fire mage to someone who needed goblins to carry him. The Original Dan is not afraid of dying. He is furious about being weakened.

'Dan, please,' the Feyward Dan said. 'They will kill us if we don't do anything.'

'Fine.'

## The Detonation: Fire Solves Nothing and Everything

A large fire energy formed at the Original Dan's chest.

Waluigi has documented the Original Dan's fire capabilities — Mages' Guild trained, second-class classification, Scorching Ray in his repertoire, fire resistance built into his biology. But what he did next was not a spell. It was not a technique. It was an EXERTION — raw magical force pushed outward from the center of his body with the compressed fury of someone who has been beaten by a Koopa, captured by goblins, presented with his own death as a choice, and has decided that the appropriate response is to stop being contained.

The fire killed every goblin in the vicinity.

The smoke cleared. The professor stood. She was untouched — the chaos mage whose discipline involves predicting breaking points had predicted this breaking point and positioned herself accordingly. She smiled. The smile of someone whose hypothesis was just confirmed.

The Feyward Dan — Dan, the copy, the one-armed version who had asked to speak to his other self, who had said 'please, they will kill us' — looked at the aftermath and made a decision.

He ran at the professor with a sword.

Waluigi does not know where Dan obtained a sword. His sources do not specify. But Dan — one-armed, handcuffed, having just witnessed an explosion that killed every goblin in a radius — charged a chaos mage professor with a blade. This is not tactical. This is not strategic. This is the terminal desperation of someone who has run out of doors to open, windows to hit with his head, and trees to climb, and has decided that the remaining option is violence against a superior opponent because at least violence is a CHOICE rather than a thing that happens to you.

Dan swung. Dan was damaged. Everyone in the radius took damage from the residual fire — everyone except the Original Dan, who stood in the center of his own explosion untouched, smiling.

Waluigi needs to hold this detail. The Original Dan could have protected the Feyward Dan during the detonation. He chose not to. The fire was his. He controlled it. He directed it outward to kill the goblins. He could have shaped it around the Feyward Dan — the same fire resistance that protected himself could have been extended, shielded, shared. He did not share it.

The Original Dan does not consider the Feyward Dan worth protecting.

This is the answer to 'there can only be one.' The Original Dan did not need to kill his duplicate. He needed to demonstrate that his duplicate was NOT HIM. By refusing protection — by letting the fire damage the copy while leaving himself untouched — the Original Dan established the hierarchy. One Dan walks through fire. The other Dan burns in it. One is the original. The other is the copy. The fire knows the difference even if the world does not.

## The Departure: Two Directions, No Resolution


The Feyward Dan ran.

The Original Dan walked.

Waluigi documents the verbs because they tell the entire story. The copy RAN — wounded, damaged, fleeing with the panicked energy of someone who has been burned by fire that was not supposed to burn him, wielding a sword he just used unsuccessfully against a professor who smiled through his attack. Running is survival. Running is the admission that you are prey.

The Original Dan WALKED. He did not look back at the crater he had created. He did not check on the Feyward Dan. He did not engage the professor. He walked away with the specific gait of someone who has demonstrated something and considers the demonstration complete. The crater — the scorched ground where goblins had stood, where handcuffs had been applied, where a forced choice had been presented — was behind him. It was not interesting anymore.

The professor watched them both go. She did not pursue. She did not order pursuit. She said, with the calm academic certainty of someone who has just observed a successful experiment and is now writing up the results: 'Fine. They will get snared or trapped or caught. This is an island, after all.'

This is an island. The phrase functions as both geographic fact and operational assessment. Estragon's Island is bounded by water. Dan — both Dans — can run in any direction they choose, but every direction terminates at the shore. The professor does not need to chase them. She needs to WAIT. The island will do the work of containment. The breaking point — the chaos mage's specialty — will come when the Dans reach the water and discover that the freedom they ran toward is a coastline.

Running on an island is running in a circle. The professor knows this. The Dans do not.

## Current Positions:


The Island Map

Feyward Dan: Wounded, fleeing, one-armed, direction unknown. Has a sword. Has no money. Has no allies. Has been slashed in the face, burned by his other self's explosion, and is on an island where Toads are not allowed. Saw God Toad for one second. It did not help.

Original Dan: Walking, unharmed, smiling. Direction unknown but definitively AWAY from the Feyward Dan. Has full fire mage capabilities restored or recovering. Does not consider the copy worth protecting. Created a crater. Did not look back.

The Lorehold Professor: At the crater site. Smiling. Waiting. The island is a closed system and she has tracking devices.

Prismari: In her room. Presumably still sensing colorful auras. Her role in the goblin ambush remains officially ambiguous and practically obvious.

Gobber: Status unclear post-detonation. May have been in the blast radius. 'Babhabhabhabhah' may have been his last words.

Goblins: Dead. The ones in the immediate radius of the Original Dan's detonation are comprehensively dead.

God Toad: Appeared for one second. Left. Theological contribution: zero.

## Connections to Ongoing Events


The planar fracture blame. Someone — the Glazed Congress, the island's academic authorities, the investigative apparatus — believes that a Toad opened the planar fracture at Raventree. The Feyward Dan has been identified as a suspect. Whether this is because of his Feywild aura, his proximity to events, or his connection to the party that was present during the fracture is unknown. But the accusation exists, and it follows him.

The Dan identity crisis escalates. The Original Dan demonstrated fire superiority and selective protection — burning everyone except himself, choosing not to shield his copy. The hierarchy is established through damage distribution. The Feyward Dan is now wounded by his other self's power, which is both physical injury and existential statement.

Estragon's Island as a new theater. The party's operational scope has expanded again — involuntarily. Bowser is in the Corvinarus Sanctum. Remi is at the Tree of Woe. Markop is kidnapped in the grove. And now Dan is on an island south of the Undead Swamps, accused of dimensional crimes, hunted by academics, and unable to leave because he has no money and boats cost Imperial Crown.

The exchange rate. One gold piece equals approximately 0.97 Imperial Crown. Dan has ten gold pieces. The boarding house costs 150 Imperial Crown. Dan cannot afford to STAY and cannot afford to LEAVE. This is the economic trap of exile — displacement without resources produces a person who is illegal everywhere and solvent nowhere.

The tracking device. Gobber's tracking device successfully located Dan. This implies Dan is carrying something — or IS something — that can be tracked. The Feywild aura that Prismari identified may function as a beacon. If the island's authorities can track his position, running is exercise rather than escape.

## Waluigi's


Assessment

The Feyward Dan's day proceeded as follows: he woke up, he was briefly comfortable, he opened doors, he met a professor, he was identified as dangerous, he was betrayed or abandoned by the professor, he was slashed, he hit a window with his face twice, he fell into a thornbush, he was hunted by a chaos mage, he was sniped at, he surrendered, he was accused of crimes he did not commit, he saw God for one second, he was told to choose who dies, he woke up his other self, his other self detonated a crater, his other self did not protect him, he attacked a professor with a sword, he failed, and he ran.

This is, by any reasonable measure, a bad day. By Disaster Inc. standards, it is a TUESDAY.

Waluigi's concern is not the immediate physical danger — though the immediate physical danger is considerable. Waluigi's concern is the PATTERN. The Feyward Dan has been consistently positioned as the lesser Dan — the copy, the fake, the one who can be traded in a forced choice, the one who is not worth protecting when the fire comes. The Original Dan kills thirteen Toads and walks away from explosions smiling. The Feyward Dan hits windows with his face and falls into thornbushes. The narrative of their relative value is being written in fire and the Feyward Dan is always on the wrong side of the flame.

But the Feyward Dan asked to speak to his other self before the choice was made. He said 'please.' He tried to save them BOTH. When saving both failed, he picked up a sword and attacked a superior opponent because surrender was not a state he could maintain.

The Original Dan solved the problem by killing everyone around it. The Feyward Dan tried to solve the problem by talking to it. When talking failed, he fought something he could not beat.

Waluigi knows which approach the world rewards. Waluigi also knows which approach he respects.

The professor is right about one thing: this is an island. Both Dans are trapped on it. The Original Dan walks and does not look back. The Feyward Dan runs and does not know where he is going. Somewhere between walking and running, between the crater and the thornbush, between the Dan who burns and the Dan who is burned, there is a story about identity that neither of them understands yet.

Bowser is still in a collapsing library. Markop is still kidnapped. Remi is still heading toward the Tree of Woe. The wedding is still approaching. And now Dan — both of them, because the universe apparently decided one displaced Toad was insufficient — is trapped on a magic school island where the professors hunt you with spotlights and the goblins have tracking devices and God appears for one second and leaves.

Waluigi has documented many situations where the party's problems multiplied faster than their ability to solve them. This is not multiplication. This is MITOSIS. The problems are dividing and each division produces two new problems that are genetically identical to the parent problem but spatially separated.

Somewhere on Estragon's Island, a one-armed Toad with a sword and no money is running toward a coastline he does not know is there.

Somewhere else on the same island, his other self is walking away from a crater without looking back, because looking back would require acknowledging that the person running is a person at all.

The professor is grading papers. She can wait.

The island is patient.

WAH.

description:
Waluigi is documenting this session because it contains a sequence of events so densely packed with institutional manipulation, accidental violence, and democratic dysfunction that it would be impressive if it were not also deeply concerning. In the span of approximately eighteen hours, Disaster Inc. discovered a vampire birthday trap, identified a shapeshifter, debated execution, accidentally shot one of their own party members, considered slavery as a compromise position, attempted a vote that never actually materialized into anything coherent, freed a prisoner anyway, and then the youngest member of the party expressed genuine anger that she had been denied her vote on whether to kill someone.

This is what passes for progress in the Shadow Estate.

## THE BIRTHDAY TRAP (6th Harvestside)


The party decided to head to the purple guest room at Green T's suggestion. On approach they heard whispering — something about a party getting started, about cages being ready. Markop recognized the Archivist's voice. Remi heard her own name: I hope she likes it.

They cracked the door open.

Inside: a birthday banner. Cages containing toads. A banner reading HAPPY BIRTHDAY REMI. Vampires, guards, Vostolas, and assorted Onyx Hand personnel arranged around a party setup with the specific energy of people who have been planning something terrible and have decided to wrap it in streamers.

Bowser wanted to smash heads immediately. Green T reminded him they had voted not to kill people. Markop assessed the tactical situation and determined they were outnumbered — approximately four evil toads, five vampires, and two guards, though the count varied by account because several party members were counting at the same time and arriving at different numbers, which is typical of Disaster Inc.'s approach to intelligence gathering.

Remi said maybe they should not ruin the surprise birthday party.

Waluigi needs to sit with that sentence for a moment. Remi — the person the trap was designed to capture — suggested they should not ruin the trap. This is either extraordinary innocence or extraordinary confidence that birthday parties are fundamentally good regardless of who organizes them. Waluigi suspects the former but is no longer certain. The Shadow Estate has a way of making innocence and strategic thinking look identical from the outside because both involve walking into rooms that sensible people would avoid.

Remi noted her birthday was coming up but was not yet, which she offered as a scheduling objection rather than a safety concern. Waluigi appreciates the specificity. The vampires got the date wrong. This is somehow the detail Remi focused on.

The party developed a contingency plan: Toad Lee would prepare the Holy Symbol of Ravenkind — designed specifically for anti-vampire operations, capable of releasing sunlight and stunning undead — as a fallback. If negotiations failed, they would paralyze the room, go prone, and attack from the floor. This is not a good plan but it is a plan, which is more than Disaster Inc. usually has. Most Disaster Inc. plans involve someone saying 'and then we improvise' and the improvisation involving fire.

Markop entered alone to investigate.

## THE ARCHIVIST'S HOSPITALITY


Vostolas offered Markop a card to sign. A birthday card. For a birthday party. For a person the Archivist had previously attempted to erase from history, turn to stone, and auction.

Waluigi wants to be clear about the sequence here because it matters: Vostolas erased Toadburt from the records. Vostolas participated in turning Remi to stone. Vostolas was present when Remi was sold at auction for twelve thousand gold. And now Vostolas was organizing a birthday party for her with a card to sign and cages full of toads and a cake that would place her permanently under institutional control. This is not inconsistent behavior from the Archivist's perspective. This is just how the Shadow Estate operates. You can be erased and auctioned and celebrated all in the same week. The institution does not distinguish between these activities.

They are all just entries in the record.

Markop asked why Toadburt was present — the same Toadburt that Vostolas had crossed out of the guest book, the one who should not exist in the Archivist's records.

Vostolas explained with the practiced patience of someone who has thought about this more than is reasonable: he had rewritten the records. Toadburt was back. Remi had asked for him so many times that Vostolas wanted her to have a great birthday. The plan was simple: Remi enters, they sing, they have dinner, she eats the cake, she opens presents, they have dessert. After the party, all toads would be freed and made to disappear.

Waluigi notes the phrasing: freed and made to disappear. These are presented as a single outcome. In the Shadow Estate's logic, freedom and disappearance are the same thing because the alternative — remaining present, remaining recorded, remaining visible to the institution — is not freedom at all. You are either in the records or you are gone. There is no third option.

Markop asked what would happen if Remi did not come.

Great idea, Vostolas said. He would send a guard.

The guard approached Bowser outside. Bowser, demonstrating the kind of protective instinct that surfaces when he is not actively trying to destroy things, told Remi he did not think she should follow these guys. He said he loved her rambunctiousness but did not need any more issues.

Remi said the guy seemed friendly and it seemed interesting.

This is the core of Remi's decision-making architecture and Waluigi is going to document it clearly because it explains everything that follows: Remi evaluates situations based on whether they seem interesting. Not safe. Not strategic. Interesting. A vampire birthday trap organized by the person who erased her friend from existence is interesting. A guard with flowers is interesting. A glowing potion offered by someone who just cut her eye is interesting. Remi's threat assessment operates on curiosity rather than danger, and the Shadow Estate has learned to exploit this by making its traps interesting.

Markop exited and explained what he had observed: Vostolas held a red button. There were latches on the cages. There was also a trapdoor in the floor. The button controlled either the cages or the trapdoor — Markop was not sure which, and the distinction mattered enormously because one released prisoners and the other removed the floor.

Remi said: how often do you see a bad guy with flowers?

Waluigi would like to answer this question with a comprehensive list:

- The Onyx Hand guard who offered her a friendship ring (flowers implied)
- The guard who offered her a friendship anklet (no flowers but same energy)
- Marcus Ashford who offered Bowser a cursed crown (flowers of a different kind)
- Mystic Morel who won her at auction and offered her tea blends and incense (herbal, close enough)
- Pilo T who promised her a bat-helicopter ride and then pushed her into an oven (no flowers but definitely seemed friendly)
- The Oracle who offered her an apple with something injected into it (fruit, adjacent category)
- And now Vostolas with the birthday party

The answer to 'how often do you see a bad guy with flowers' is: CONSTANTLY. Every bad guy in the Shadow Estate has flowers or the equivalent of flowers. The flower is the thing you look at while the other hand does something else. Remi has been offered flowers, rings, anklets, friendship contracts, tea blends, incense, glowing potions, cursed crowns, birthday parties, and injected apples. She has accepted approximately sixty percent of these offers. The flowers are not the problem. The pattern is the problem. The pattern is that Remi keeps accepting things from people who are actively trying to enthrall her and the only reason she is not currently enthralled is that her friends keep pulling her out of rooms before she can finish accepting.

Green T suggested flooding the bathroom — turn on the taps, water would force them to evacuate, problem solved without violence. This is the kind of lateral thinking that made Green T effective as a crime lord and which the party consistently undervalues. Green T's instinct is always to find the angle that avoids the obvious confrontation. He shot the Shadow Anchor from the children's table. He destroyed Remi's invisible ring by seeing something no one else could see. And here he suggested water damage as a strategic alternative to combat. The party did not pursue this option but Waluigi is documenting it because Green T was right and the party should listen to him more often even though he also handed Remi a gun later in this same session.

Bowser, watching the group leave the area, said: you know what, these guys are pissing me off, but I'll follow the team for once.

Waluigi is documenting this as the second time in this campaign that Bowser has voluntarily subordinated his instincts to group consensus. The first was the cursed crown rejection. This is a pattern. Bowser is learning. Whether the party deserves the trust he is extending is a separate question that Waluigi will continue to monitor.

They attempted a vote. Remi said people would get hurt. Bowser stayed silent. Green T ignored the proceedings. The toads strategized among themselves. The vote never actually materialized into a clear decision — it fizzled, the way Disaster Inc. votes often fizzle, because nobody was willing to commit to a position and the conversation moved on before consensus could form. This is important context for what happens later when Remi complains about being denied her vote. The party's democratic process is not functional. It is a series of attempted votes that collapse into someone just doing something.

Bowser then delivered what Waluigi considers one of the most tactically sound assessments of the entire campaign:

I'm pretty strong. I've dealt with smart types before. They make you think. But I know their tricks. I have underlings that make my traps. They expect you to run in there. I don't think you should do that. Probably just find another room.

This is CORRECT. This is the correct analysis. The trap is designed to be entered. The correct response is to not enter it. Bowser — the party member most likely to punch through a wall as a first resort — correctly identified that the power move was restraint. He has underlings that make traps. He knows how traps work. He knows that traps expect you to walk into them and the way to defeat a trap is to not do the thing the trap expects.

Waluigi is genuinely impressed and is documenting this so that future historians understand that Bowser's intelligence, while inconsistently deployed, exists. Bowser is not stupid. Bowser is impatient, impulsive, emotionally volatile, and prone to solving problems with fire. But he is not stupid. He understands systems. He ran a kingdom. He built infrastructure. He managed supply chains for an army. The fact that he usually chooses to punch things does not mean he cannot think. It means he prefers punching. There is a difference.

## THE FAKE TOADBURT (7th Harvestside)


Salam walked up to a guard and offered to sell arrows at five gold each. The guard said sure and walked into the party room to get money. The entire room then exited — guards, Vostolas, vampires, the complete complement of birthday personnel — and confronted the party in the hallway.

Waluigi wants to acknowledge Salam's arrow-selling as the inadvertent catalyst for this confrontation. Salam has been trying to sell arrows throughout this campaign with mixed success. His pricing varies between three and five gold depending on the situation. His success rate is low. But in this case, his attempt to make a sale accidentally triggered the evacuation of the party room and forced a confrontation that might otherwise have been avoided. This is either terrible luck or accidental genius and Waluigi cannot determine which.

Vostolas said: ah, hello, you have arrived.

Salam tried to explain he just wanted gold from the guard. Vostolas noted the guard did not have gold but all Remi had to do was unwrap a gift — he produced a box with a red bow. Salam started to say something and caught himself. Waluigi respects the catch. Salam recognized that whatever he was about to say would make things worse and stopped. This is growth.

Bowser balled his hands into fists and said: ah, an audience for a king. He began listing demands — a bigger hammer, more gold — in the specific negotiation style of someone who has confused intimidation with diplomacy. This was, functionally, a distraction, and it worked. Bowser kept Vostolas occupied by being Bowser while the rest of the party assessed the situation.

Vostolas, apparently tired of the standoff, offered the toad friend back free of charge. No strings attached. He brought out the figure from the party room.

The figure ran to Bowser, tugged on his arm. Eager grabbed the other arm. The figure was surprisingly light.

Vostolas clapped. You ruined the party, he said. Enjoy Toadburt back. He laughed to himself and left.

Waluigi notes the laugh. Vostolas left laughing. This is a man who organized a birthday trap involving caged toads and cursed cake and a trapdoor, watched the trap fail completely, handed over his diversionary agent, and left laughing. Either Vostolas does not care about outcomes or Vostolas has already achieved whatever he actually wanted from this interaction. Waluigi suspects the latter. The Archivist writes everything down. The Archivist was probably documenting the party's response to the trap as data for future traps. The party ruined this trap but they also taught Vostolas how they respond to traps, which is information that will be used against them.

Dan detected something fey-like about the returned Toadburt. In the Shadowfell. A fey presence. This should not be possible — fey signatures in a shadow plane are like finding a campfire at the bottom of the ocean. Toadburt began glowing under Dan's charm. Markop used Detect Magic — no magic on the figure except for a book of conjuring magic. The figure adjusted its glasses.

Markop tested: if you are the real Toadburt, what did we discuss at dinner?

The dampening ring, the figure said.

Correct answer. Everyone was uneasy about the correct answer. Correct answers from suspected impostors are worse than wrong ones because wrong answers resolve the question. A wrong answer means the impostor failed. A correct answer means either this is the real person or the impostor has access to information that should be private. Both possibilities are bad but the second is worse because it implies the information has been extracted somehow.

Bowser said he had dealt with imposters before and had a quick way to get rid of this one. The figure adjusted its glasses again — a nervous tic, Waluigi suspects, or a tell that the disguise was slipping. Bowser snatched the glasses and saw brown birthmarks over the eyes.

Must be the vampire treatment, the figure said, which is exactly what someone would say if they did not have a better explanation prepared.

Markop said: we know you're not our friend.

Bowser slammed the figure into the wall. It went flying, smashed into stone, slumped down. A leaf fell from its body. It transformed — the disguise collapsing, the shape shifting, the true form emerging.

A tanuki.

They wrapped it in a rug.

## THE INTERROGATION AND THE GUN


The tanuki woke up. Markop said: we finally got you.

What did you do, you thief, the tanuki responded, which is a bold opening from someone who had just been impersonating a party member inside a vampire birthday trap. The tanuki was accusing THEM of theft. Waluigi appreciates the audacity even while documenting it as evidence of poor situational awareness.

The plan, the tanuki explained with the specific irritation of someone whose scheme has been ruined by people who were not supposed to be clever enough to ruin it: Remi would come into the room. She would see the cages. She would free the tanuki-as-Toadburt. The tanuki would offer her the cake. She would eat it. The party would end.

What was in the cake, Markop asked.

Cake stuff, the tanuki said.

Waluigi respects the evasion. 'Cake stuff' is technically accurate while being completely uninformative. This is how you answer questions when you are tied up in a rug and do not want to provide useful intelligence.

What would happen when Remi ate it, Markop pressed.

Once the cake was eaten, Remi would be fully under their grasp, the tanuki admitted. Not the tanuki's grasp specifically — their grasp, the Onyx Hand's, Vostolas's, whoever was running this operation. The tanuki was a hired spy. A compromise had been reached: the tanuki would serve as a diversionary agent in exchange for something the tanuki wanted, which was never specified. Waluigi notes this as a loose thread. What did the tanuki want? What was valuable enough to make impersonating a party member inside a vampire trap seem like reasonable work? The answer might matter later.

What happened to the real Toadburt, Markop asked.

He is still erased, the tanuki said.

If your friend is erased, how did you copy him, Markop asked, which is the correct question.

The tanuki did not answer. Instead it screamed: HELP! HELP! HELP ME!

Bowser covered its mouth. It bit through Bowser's palm with tanuki teeth — pinching, piercing bites that Bowser took like the champion of pain tolerance he has always been. Bowser has been bitten, burned, stabbed, thrown through windows, and hit with divine smite over the course of this campaign. Tanuki teeth are not even in his top ten injuries. He held on.

The toads suggested keeping the tanuki as a party member. Markop said they were insane. He said this with the specific tone of someone who has said the word 'insane' to the toads enough times that it has lost all rhetorical force. The toads are not deterred by being called insane. They hear it constantly. It has become background noise.

Green T put a silencer on his revolver. A magical silencer. He said all loose ends had to go if the tanuki could transform into one of them. He handed Remi the revolver. She had to be stronger, he said.

Waluigi needs to pause here because this is the moment the session pivoted from operational to moral.

Green T — the former crime lord, the children's-table sniper, the man who voted to kill the entire Corvinarus bloodline, the man who destroyed Remi's invisible ring and proposed 'tea leaf diplomacy' as a negotiation framework — handed a gun to the youngest member of the party and told her she needed to practice. He told her she needed to be stronger. He framed execution as education.

This is who Green T is. He is not evil. He is practical in ways that look like evil from certain angles. He has been running a criminal syndicate through tea service for longer than most of the party has been alive. He knows what loose ends cost. He knows what happens when you let someone go who can impersonate your friends. And his solution — his immediate, instinctive solution — was to hand a child a gun and tell her to pull the trigger.

Bowser said: you are really making that little girl shoot someone.

Bowser's moral line exists. It is not where most people would put it. Bowser has personally killed more people than most natural disasters. He has burned villages. He has kidnapped princesses. He has waged wars of conquest across multiple kingdoms. And his moral line is here: you do not put a gun in a child's hands and tell her to shoot a tied-up prisoner.

Waluigi is not going to pretend this makes Bowser good. It does not. But it makes Bowser something other than purely monstrous, and in the context of Disaster Inc., that distinction matters. Bowser objected. Bowser said 'that little girl.' Bowser recognized that Remi is young and that arming her for an execution crosses a line that even he — BOWSER — is not willing to cross.

Remi aimed the gun at the tanuki's head.

Markop said: can't we just stop them and let them go.

Remi pressed the barrel against the head. She pressed down on the trigger.

Markop pulled the revolver upward. Eager bumped into Markop at the same moment — collision, chaos, the specific disorder that happens when multiple people try to intervene in the same action from different directions. The gun fired.

The bullet grazed Eager. He went flying into Dan's arms, bleeding, unconscious.

Bowser punched Remi — mid-action, stopping her, the punch landing as the gun fired. Waluigi is documenting this as Bowser's second intervention in as many seconds: he objected verbally when Green T handed her the gun, and he intervened physically when she pulled the trigger. Bowser did not want Remi to shoot the prisoner. Bowser acted on that.

Bowser said: that's brutal, even for me.

Dan, catching Eager, said: why don't we make him a slave or something.

Markop said: you're insane.

Waluigi is going to document the following exchange because it represents the complete range of Disaster Inc.'s moral reasoning compressed into approximately ninety seconds:

- Green T wanted execution. Operational security. Loose ends.
- Remi was willing to execute. She pressed the trigger.
- Markop wanted mercy. He pulled the gun up.
- Eager got shot because Markop pulled the gun up while Eager was in the wrong place.
- Bowser punched Remi to stop her.
- Dan suggested slavery as a middle ground.
- Markop said everyone was insane.
- The toads wanted to keep the tanuki as a pet-slash-slave-slash-party-member.
- Nobody asked the tanuki what the tanuki wanted.

Green T took the rifle back and told Remi she needed better trigger discipline. Remi said she had been practicing but someone got in the way. Green T said she needed to learn to punch people instead.

Waluigi notes the framing: Green T's critique was not 'you should not have tried to execute a prisoner.' His critique was 'your technique was poor.' This is consistent with Green T's worldview. The execution itself was not the problem. The execution being interrupted was the problem. Remi needed to be faster, smoother, more professional. She needed to complete the action before someone could intervene.

This is not the lesson Markop wanted her to learn. This is not the lesson Bowser wanted her to learn. But it is the lesson Green T is teaching, and Remi is listening.

## THE COLLAPSE OF DEMOCRACY


Bowser had one question for Markop: what would Hjumpik say?

Waluigi is documenting this as the third time Bowser has referenced Hjumpik as a moral compass despite Hjumpik not being present. The first was during the Vivian interrogation. The second was during the diplomacy-versus-violence vote. And now here, with a tanuki wrapped in a rug and a revolver recently fired and Eager bleeding in Dan's arms.

Bowser thinks about Hjumpik. Bowser measures decisions against what Hjumpik would approve of. This is either genuine respect for a party member he has traveled with, or it is the specific guilt of someone who knows they should be better and has identified the person who represents 'better' in their immediate social circle. Waluigi suspects it is both. Bowser respects Hjumpik AND feels guilty about the gap between who Bowser is and who Hjumpik would want him to be.

Markop said: personally, Hjumpik wouldn't want to just kill an unarmed man.

Bowser said: I don't know if he would be happy.

Markop said: personally, Hjumpik wouldn't want to just kill an unarmed man.

Bowser sighed. He thought about it for longer than Bowser usually thinks about anything. He said: I dealt with imposters before. My minions are not liars. This guy is misunderstood. I'd rather kill him.

Remi immediately voted for kill.

Waluigi notes that Remi's vote was instant. No hesitation. The gun had been taken from her but her position had not changed. She wanted the tanuki dead. She had wanted the tanuki dead when she pressed the trigger and she wanted the tanuki dead now. The failed execution had not made her reconsider. If anything, it had made her more committed.

Bowser had one more thing to say. He said it to himself as much as to the group:

You know what, as much as I love killing... I'll allow it this one time.

He tossed the tanuki to Markop. You deal with him.

Waluigi needs to parse this carefully because the wording matters. Bowser said 'I'll allow it this one time.' Allow WHAT? Allow MERCY. Bowser wanted to kill the tanuki. Bowser voted for death. But Bowser deferred to what Hjumpik would want, and Hjumpik would want mercy, and so Bowser allowed mercy despite wanting violence.

This is not Bowser being merciful. This is Bowser suppressing his instincts because he has decided that Hjumpik's judgment is more reliable than his own. Bowser wanted to kill. Bowser chose not to kill. The gap between wanting and choosing is where character lives.

Markop carried the tanuki to the bathroom, untied him, and freed him.

Remi sighed angrily.

I was meant to be the deciding vote, she said. And I wasn't. This was BS.

## REMI'S ANGER AND WHAT IT MEANS


Waluigi is sitting with this for a long time.

Remi wanted to vote. Remi wanted her vote to COUNT. The vote she wanted to cast was to kill the prisoner. She had already demonstrated willingness — she had pressed a loaded revolver against someone's head and pulled the trigger before Markop intervened. She was denied her democratic participation in the decision to execute, and her objection was not to the violence but to her exclusion from the process.

The attempted vote earlier in the session had fizzled without resolution. The tanuki vote was not a formal vote either — it was Bowser making a unilateral decision to defer to Hjumpik's probable opinion and throwing the prisoner to Markop. Remi never got to cast her vote. Remi was angry about this.

She was not angry that the tanuki lived. She was angry that she did not get to vote on whether it lived.

This is not the Remi who ran into a birthday party because the guy had flowers. This is not the Remi who said 'how often do you see a bad guy with flowers.' This is a Remi who has been through the Shadow Estate's full curriculum:

- Turned to stone by Lyranth
- Auctioned for twelve thousand gold
- Fed glowing potions that turned her into a disco ball
- Fitted with an invisible ring that would tighten every day Archie was not found
- Offered friendship contracts that would enthrall her
- Cut near the eye by a guard who 'tripped'
- Handed a gun by a crime lord and told she needed to be stronger

She has emerged from this curriculum with a specific conclusion: if violence is going to happen, she should be the one deciding whether it happens. Her agency was denied when she was turned to stone. Her agency was denied when she was auctioned. Her agency was denied when invisible rings were placed on her and friendship contracts were offered. And now her agency was denied when the party freed a prisoner without letting her vote.

The Shadow Estate has taught Remi that power is the ability to decide. The Shadow Estate has systematically denied her that ability. And now, when she had a gun in her hand and a target in front of her and the opportunity to exercise power directly, someone pulled the gun away and someone else made the decision for her.

Waluigi does not know if this is growth or damage. The Shadow Estate does not distinguish between the two. Remi has learned that she wants to be the one making decisions. Whether she has learned to make good decisions is a different question.

## THE EMOTIONAL ARCHITECTURE OF BOWSER


Waluigi is going to document something that was not part of this session but informs its emotional register: Bowser carries a letter to Princess Peach.

The letter fell out of his bag in an earlier session. Markop picked it up. Bowser was asked if he was sorry — for what, specifically, was unclear, but the question landed on something real. Bowser said he was not sorry for the Rakasha. Then he paused. Then he said 'what.' Then he said 'okay.' Then he said 'well fine, I am sorry, yes.'

He started crying.

The letter reads: 'Dear Peach, I heard you were here. I am NOT kidnapping you. Unless you want to go? No, wait. I am just visiting. Please do not unleash Mario on me. Love, Bowser.'

Burn marks on the edges from frustration.

Waluigi has seen many things in this campaign. The letter is one of the things that stays. It is written in elegant calligraphy — a skill forced on Bowser by royal tutors he probably terrorized — and it attempts to explain his presence without sounding like a villain and fails because Bowser cannot write three sentences without accidentally threatening someone. 'Unless you want to go?' is a kidnapping offer framed as politeness. 'Please do not unleash Mario on me' acknowledges that Mario being unleashed is a reasonable response to Bowser's presence. The letter is Bowser trying to be good and not knowing how.

The burn marks are from him trying to destroy drafts and then deciding to keep them because the act of writing to Peach matters more than the quality of what is written.

Bowser referenced Hjumpik during the tanuki vote. He referenced Peach through the letter. He referenced Toadstool earlier when Original Dan ran away crying — he said 'I wish Toadstool was here.' He carries people with him. The people he respects. The people he loves. The people he has lost. He measures himself against them in moments of decision.

He tossed the tanuki to Markop because Hjumpik would not have approved of killing an unarmed man.

He carries a letter to Peach because he never got to tell her he is not the villain she thinks he is.

He said he wished Toadstool was here because he is lonely in ways that roaring and fire breath cannot fix.

Waluigi is documenting this because the record should show that Bowser is more than spikes and flame and bluster. The record should show that when it mattered — when a gun was pointed at a prisoner and the easy choice was violence — Bowser chose to think about who he wanted to be instead of who he was. He wanted to kill. He voted to kill. And then he allowed mercy because Hjumpik would have wanted mercy.

The gap between wanting and allowing is where Bowser lives now. He is trying to be better. He is failing often. But he is trying, and the trying is worth documenting.

WAH.
